noticeTitle: Belgium – Sewage, refuse, cleaning and environmental services – Interactions between Climate Action and Defence
procedureTitle: Interactions between Climate Action and Defence
description: The objective of the study is to analyse how EU climate action and defence policy interact in the context of Russia’s aggression, by identifying synergies, trade-offs and risks. It aims to: • assess how the defence sector can contribute to EU climate goals (mitigation, resilience, nature restoration and dual-use clean technologies), • examine how climate policies can contribute to and impact on defence capabilities and readiness, the defence industry, build public resilience against hybrid threats, and budgetary priorities. The study is intended to provide evidence for aligning rearmament and defence readiness with EU climate neutrality and resilience objectives and aligning the design of climate policies with defence needs.

noticeTitle: Belgium – Sewage, refuse, cleaning and environmental services – Advancing Climate Finance for Global Transition Pathways Towards Carbon Neutrality and Climate Resilient Development
procedureTitle: Advancing Climate Finance for Global Transition Pathways Towards Carbon Neutrality and Climate Resilient Development
description: Achieving the transition towards carbon-neutral and climate-resilient development necessitates a comprehensive understanding of the financial needs, targeted investment areas, and the deployment of effective financial instruments on a global scale. Moreover, reforming the international financial architecture is crucial to facilitate and support this transition. The action should explore these critical dimensions of climate finance, including the identification of tools to monitor climate financial flows (public and private, international and domestic) as a foundation for evidence-based decision-making. The action should cover the following elements at global level with differentiation by geographic area with a focus on SIDS and LDCs: 1) Identification of Financial Needs for Climate Transition 2) Targeted Areas for Investment 3) Financial Instruments and Mechanisms 4) Reforming the International Financial Architecture 5) Monitoring Climate Financial Flows 6) Mobilizing Private Sector Investment. Form of Funding: Procurement

noticeTitle: Belgium – Research consultancy services – Support for the review by the Commission concerning the implementation of ICAO’s CORSIA, and for Commission reports on certain types of flights, social impacts, and air connectivity of islands, remote territories and Iceland
procedureTitle: Support for the review by the Commission concerning the implementation of ICAO’s CORSIA, and for Commission reports on certain types of flights, social impacts, and air connectivity of islands, remote territories and Iceland
description: Provide for support for the revision of the ETS Directive for aviaiton This call for tender requests analytical services for the review by the Commission concerning implementation by third countries of the International Civil Aviation Organization’s (ICAO) measure ‘Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation’ (CORSIA), as required by Article 28b (2) of Directive 2003/87/EC (hereinafter, "the Directive"), and including Article 25a(7) and Article 30(8). It also requests analysis on environmental and climate impacts, and ways to reduce those, of short-haul flights, private- and business jet flights, as defined in Article 30(8)(a) and (b) of the Directive, and as required in Article 30(8). It also requests analysis of the social impacts of this Directive and connectivity, as required by Article 30(8)(c) and (d), the latter should also take into account Iceland. All sectors of the economy, including international aviation, need to contribute to reduce greenhouse gas emissions so that we can comply with our commitment to the temperature goals of the Paris Agreement. CO2 emissions from aviation have been included in the EU emissions trading system (EU ETS) since 2012. Since then, the scope of the EU ETS has been restricted to intra-European flights to facilitate progress at ICAO. With the revision of the EU ETS for aviation, co-legislators have tasked the Commission to report on the environmental integrity of CORSIA by 1 July 2026. The report will be accompanied by a legislative proposal, where appropriate, to amend the ETS in a way that is consistent with the Paris Agreement temperature goal, the Union’s economy-wide greenhouse gas emission reduction commitment for 2030 and climate neutrality by 2050 at the latest, and with the aim of preserving the environmental integrity and effectiveness of the Union’s climate action. One part of this tender focuses on the analysis to support the report on environmental integrity of CORSIA, which co-legislators have tasked the Commission to provide by 1 July 2026. The successful candidate will provide analytical support for this assessment, notably an overview of implementation by third countries of CORSIA, as well how this affects general ambition in relation to targets under the Paris Agreement. The other part of this tender concerns analysis for certain flights. For intra-European flights between 2024-26, the European institutions have strengthened the ETS aviation rules to ensure that aviation contributes to the more ambitious target of achieving net emission reductions of at least 55% by 2030, compared to 1990 levels. The amendment of the Directive includes specific elements for the Commission to evaluate as part of its Carbon Market Report in 2026. While the Commission will carry out the evaluation independently, analysis is needed on impacts of short-haul, business- and private jet flights, as well social impacts of this Directive and air connectivity. On connectivity, the analysis should also include Iceland.

procedureTitle: Support for the evaluation of the EU emissions trading system (EU ETS) and the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) and for the 2026 review of the EU ETS and MSR
description: The general objective of this contract is to support DG CLIMA in the evaluation of the EU ETS and the MSR, and in the review of certain elements due in 2026, by providing timely and high-quality input for supporting the Commission in drafting its own evaluation report and an impact assessment, in an almost parallel manner, in line with the Commission's Better Regulation Guidelines. The three specific objectives of this support contract are: (1) Support the Commission in drafting an “evaluation staff working document”, in particular assessing the effectiveness, relevance, efficiency, coherence and EU added value of the selected aspects of the ETS Directive and of the MSR Decision, as well as identifying areas of further action in this policy area in view of current and future climate change objectives. The selected aspects are: (i) Carbon leakage protection measures for non-CBAM sectors; and (ii) MSR in respect of ETS1. In addition, the consultant may be asked to carry out ad-hoc tasks related to the assessment of other interconnected elements that are to be included in the evaluation. (2) Support the Commission in drafting an “Impact Assessment staff working document" for revising selected aspects of the ETS Directive and the MSR Decision, by setting out a range of policy options and providing the evidence base for and the impacts of each option on the following topics: (i) MSR; (ii) negative emissions; (iii) accounting and double counting of non-permanent CCU; (iv) municipal waste incineration and other waste management processes; (v) the feasibility of lowering the 20 MW total rated thermal input thresholds; (vi) linkages between the EU ETS and other carbon markets; and (vii) carbon leakage protection measures for non-CBAM sectors. In addition, the consultant may be asked to carry out ad-hoc tasks related to the assessment of other interconnected elements that are to be included in the impact assessment. (3) Design, carry out and analyse the results of the public consultation on the evaluation and impact assessment of points 1 and 2.

Description: The general objective of this contract is to support DG CLIMA in the evaluation of the EU ETS and the MSR, and in the review of certain elements due in 2026, by providing timely and high-quality input for supporting the Commission in drafting its own evaluation report and an impact assessment, in an almost parallel manner, in line with the Commission's Better Regulation Guidelines. The three specific objectives of this support contract are: (1) Support the Commission in drafting an “evaluation staff working document”, in particular assessing the effectiveness, relevance, efficiency, coherence and EU added value of the selected aspects of the ETS Directive and of the MSR Decision, as well as identifying areas of further action in this policy area in view of current and future climate change objectives. The selected aspects are: (i) Carbon leakage protection measures for non-CBAM sectors; and (ii) MSR in respect of ETS1. In addition, the consultant may be asked to carry out ad-hoc tasks related to the assessment of other interconnected elements that are to be included in the evaluation. (2) Support the Commission in drafting an “Impact Assessment staff working document" for revising selected aspects of the ETS Directive and the MSR Decision, by setting out a range of policy options and providing the evidence base for and the impacts of each option on the following topics: (i) MSR; (ii) negative emissions; (iii) accounting and double counting of non-permanent CCU; (iv) municipal waste incineration and other waste management processes; (v) the feasibility of lowering the 20 MW total rated thermal input thresholds; (vi) linkages between the EU ETS and other carbon markets; and (vii) carbon leakage protection measures for non-CBAM sectors. In addition, the consultant may be asked to carry out ad-hoc tasks related to the assessment of other interconnected elements that are to be included in the impact assessment. (3) Design, carry out and analyse the results of the public consultation on the evaluation and impact assessment of points 1 and 2.

noticeTitle: Belgium – Environmental services – Support for the evaluation of the EU emissions trading system (EU ETS) and the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) and for the 2026 review of the EU ETS and MSR
procedureTitle: Support for the evaluation of the EU emissions trading system (EU ETS) and the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) and for the 2026 review of the EU ETS and MSR
description: The contract is to support DG CLIMA in the evaluation of the EU ETS and the review of certain elements due in 2026. An evaluation of the ETS Directive and the MSR Decision is required on the basis of the ‘evaluate first’ principle, i.e. before revisions of EU legislation. The evaluation will be limited to those issues which have not been subject, in part or in full, to major changes in the last revision of the ETS Directive (primarily free allocation for non-CBAM sectors, the Modernisation Fund, and the MSR), and any other elements that are maintained. Provisions that have been subject to major amendments should not be evaluated, as conclusions on their performance from 2015 (or 2021) cannot be addressed if other changes were made in the meantime. Four elements of the EU ETS are due for review in 2026: 1. Market Stability Reserve. For this review it will be necessary to: a. Analyse current market actors, hedging behaviour and stability risks in EU ETS b. Analyse options for changing the rules of the MSR (thresholds, intake rate) compared to baseline of continued policy c. Analyse, proportionate to political priority, more radical changes to MSR operation d. ex-ante analysis of ETS2 MSR operation 2. Negative emissions: how negative emissions resulting from greenhouse gases that are removed from the atmosphere and safely and permanently stored (BECCS and DACCS) could be accounted for and how those negative emissions could be covered by emissions trading , if appropriate, including a clear scope and strict criteria for such trading, and safeguards to ensure that such removals do not offset necessary emission reductions in accordance with the Climate Law. While reducing emissions remains the absolute priority in the coming years and decades in climate action, carbon removals will become increasingly important over time to deal with hardest to abate emissions and to reach negative emissions. 3. Accounting and double counting of non-permanent CCU: whether all greenhouse gas emissions covered by the ETS are effectively accounted for, and whether double counting is effectively avoided; in particular, regarding greenhouse gas emissions which are considered to have been captured and utilised in a product non-permanently. 4. Inclusion of municipal waste incineration (MWI) and other waste management processes: the feasibility of including municipal waste incineration installations in the EU ETS, with a view to their inclusion from 2028, and the possibility of including in the EU ETS other waste management processes, in particular landfills which create methane and nitrous oxide emissions. Regarding MWI, the report must to take into account: o the importance of all sectors contributing to emission reductions and potential diversion of waste towards disposal by landfilling in the Union and waste exports to third countries, and measures to prevent potential diversion of waste. o the effects on the internal market, o potential distortions of competition, o environmental integrity, o alignment with the objectives of the Waste Framework Directive, o robustness and accuracy of the monitoring and calculation of emissions. Topics 2, 3, and 4 are interconnected subjects that require an overall reassessment of how the ETS works. The three topics need to be seen in context of a CO2 value chain and move towards a circular carbon system in an ETS with a cap going to zero. For example, examining how the ETS treats embedded emissions in chemical products, the treatment of e-fuels and other non-permanent CCU products in case several waste management processes or MWI are included in the ETS, and the creation of a simple CO2 value chain in which removals may or may not be included in the ETS but part of the liability for reversals will be covered by the ETS in it's CCS activities. The contract will also require examining the interplay with environmental policies for both waste and the treatment of non-permanent CCU products.

procedureTitle: Support to the Commission for the assessment of submitted National Implementation Measures
description: Directive 2003/87/EC (the EU ETS Directive) has been revised for the allocation period 2026 to 2030. In September 2024, Member States will have to submit to the Commission the list of installations covered by the Directive, as well as any free allocation for the period 2026 to 2030 for each installation in the list, calculated in accordance with Union-wide harmonised free allocation rules. The data collected, referred to as National Implementation Measures (NIMs), must be verified and assessed by the Member States and thereafter submitted to the Commission in September 2024 that will, in turn, perform an assessment to determine compliance with the relevant legal provisions. Given the technical nature of the assessment, the amount of numbers that must be checked, the complexity of the free allocation rules, the formal and informal communication with the Member States and the short timeframe for concluding this work, as well as our previous experience, we foresee the need for support from a contractor for carrying out the assessment of the data. This will be extremely time-consuming work and also very important, as free allocation will have a financial impact on the participating companies. Moreover, it will be crucial to ensure comparably robust data across Member States, so a thorough assessment will need to be performed.

procedureTitle: Analytical capacity for international climate action (renewable)
description: GHG emissions need to be reduced by 43% in 2030 compared to 2019 levels to keep a 1.5-degree pathway in reach. The gap in emission reductions until 2030 and beyond is both a challenge of raising ambition as well as realising implementation. Analytical capacity based on greenhouse gas emissions modelling is providing the foundation to overcome both ambition and implementation gaps as it contributes to a knowledge base necessary to design impactful climate policies and regulation. Continuous modelling capacity is therefore required to answer the urgent call to increase climate action before 2030 and analyse new NDCs as well as new and updated long-term strategies for low carbon development (LT-LEDS), aiming at CO2 neutrality around 2050. The contracting authority requires access to state-of-the-art analytical capacity on global climate change mitigation action, as well as quantitative analysis and model-derived scenarios of global climate change mitigation.
